Phase 1 Site Assessment of a portion of the Portland Road Widening Project area. Records indicated that the property at 2685 Portland Road NE, most recently occupied by the La Gran Cantina restaurant, had previously been the site of a fueling station dating back to 1926

On May 21, 2001, a site investigation was completed in the City right-of-way surrounding the property to the east and north.  Five direct-push borings to depths of up to 23 feet below ground surface were advanced.  The borings were advanced along both Pine Street and Portland Road near the La Gran Cantina.  Soil and Groundwater samples were collected during the site activities.  During the site investagation a 1,500-gallon USt was found.  It was located on the northeastern side of the La Gran Cantina.  The fill pipe was located in the sidewalk along Pine Street.  A sample was collected from the tank.  the laboratory results indicated the presence of weathered gasoline and a trace of weathered diesel.  the UST was decommissioned by removalon April 8, 2003, and was identified as a heating oil tank that apparently had also been used for the storave of other miscellaneous petroleum products.  Approximately 3.4 tons of diesel-impacted soil was transported to teh Hillsboro Landfill in Hillsboro, Oregon.

On May 13, 2003, a second abandoned UST was found.  The tank was empty and determined to be unregulated.  The excavation was approximately 8 feet wide, 12 feet long and 8 feet deep.  A total of 159.64 tons of petroleum-contaminated soil wlere removed from the vicinity of the UST.  The petroleum-contaminated soil was transported to Waste Mangement's Riverbend Landfill in McMinnville, Oregon

On April 28 and 29, 2005, GeoEnginers supervised the advancement of 14 direct-push exploration borings.  The 14 borings were installed along Portland Road NE, and in the new access road.  Sixteen soil samples were collected with only one soil sampl, SB-18 (19-20 feet below ground surface), exhibiting detectable levels of PAHs  Grab samples of groundwater were collected from ten samples at concentration ranging between 250 ppb and 5,070 ppb

In July 2006, to collect new data and evaluate the site’s Orphan potential, DEQ sampled three existing drinking water wells, but not existing monitoring wells, using DEQ administered EPA LUST grant funds.  Sampling results for petroleum-related constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes (BTEX) were below levels recorded in the 1990s.  However, concentrations of 1,2-dichloroethane (EDC), a common “lead scavenger” in petroleum, remained above DEQ risk-based concentrations (RBCs) for the drinking water pathway in two drinking water wells.

DEQ sampled existing drinking water wells in October 2006 and June 2007 using grant funds from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to collect new data and evaluate the site as a potential Orphan candidate.   Most of the previously installed monitoring wells were either destroyed or could not be located in the field.  

Two adjacent domestic wells, including the shared Store/residence well and the well located downgradient of the site were also sampled to evaluate impacts to the drinking water aquifer.  The Store well was sampled in October 2006 and in June 2007.  The residence well was only sampled in October 2006.  

The groundwater extraction well (MW-3) was sampled in June 2007 following the TCR activities that removed the pump and piping from the well.  However during field activities, the vault that the well was completed within appears to have been impacted by shallow groundwater and surface water infiltration directly into the protective vault.  During June 2007, the vault was completely filled with water (4-feet x 4-feet x 4-feet).  DEQ subsequently removed approximately 100 gallons of water from the vault and exposed the well casing.  There was some visual soil staining present within the vault and an apparent sheen that appeared to be coming from the soil surround the vault.  No well cap was present on the casing and DEQ subsequently attempted to purge the well.  The well appeared to have been heavily silted to approximately 8.5 feet bgs of a total depth 15 feet bgs.  The well also did not appear to recharging and subsequent sample results should be evaluated and used with caution.

All groundwater samples were submitted for total petroleum hydrocarbon (TPH) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) analysis.  None of the domestic wells water samples had any detections during either sampling event.  

The extraction well results indicated a positive TPH detection, although the TPH specific result was below the lab detection level of 400 micrograms per liter (ug/l).  Positive detections of toluene (97 ug/l) and 1,2,4-trimethylbenzen (16.7 ug/l).  These results are likely biased low due to the amount of water in the vault and likely surface water infiltration.

The majority of the work at this Site has been performed under 23-06-0475.  A review of the files and communication between DEQ and Wohlers Environmental Services, Inc.,  indicate that 23-79-0001 may have been related to the release on a nearby property (the former Unocal Bulk Plant #0794) located at 76 SE 4th Street and East Idaho.  This property, referred to as ECSI #517 was recently issued a conditional No Further Action (NFA) in the fall of 2003.  

1.    A 1979 complaint initiated an investigation into the source of the vapors.  The Poole facility was tank tightness tested (TTT) as part of the investigation. There was an apparent catastrophic release of 2,000 gallons of gasoline while the TTT was being conducted and was the basis of the 1979 release report to the DEQ.  A previously unknown manifold UST was found when the UST was uncovered to search for the source of the release. The testing pushed the fuel into the manifold tank giving the appearance of a major release. There was no catastrophic release.  However, while excavating the UST contaminated soil and groundwater were discovered at the Poole facility from earlier releases over time. This spill discovery became the release under the LUST number 23-79-0001. 

2.    The spill from the Unocal Bulk Plant was on May 25, 1983. The release was estimated at 20,000 gallons of gasoline.  A test pit, groundwater sampling and nine well investigation followed in 1984. The relevant results show no odor, nor any soil or groundwater contamination between the bulk plant and business west of the bulk plant.    Sampling of the bulk plant towards the Poole facility showed six inches of discolored soil, odor, and gasoline in the soil. The groundwater flow direction is to the north/northeast.  No contamination was found to the south of the Poole facility. The available data leads to the conclusion that the Poole facility is the source of contamination for the site itself and the release(s) being old. There is nothing to suggest a recent release from the Poole facility, nor a migration of contamination from another source. 

3.    The work completed at the Unocal site from 1983 through 2003 included extensive investigation, monitoring, and remedial actions including product recovery and air sparging.  A record of decision (ROD) for the Unocal site was completed in 2003 that evaluated remaining concentration risk and pathways and it was determined that the Unocal site could be conditionally closed with deed restrictions.

DEQ recommends an administrative closure for 23-79-0001 as the majority of work has been conducted under 23-06-0475, the historic releases are not easily separable and any additional work will be incorporated as LUST spill 23-06-0475.

An additional five test pits were completed to varying depths to further characterize the site.  The February 1990 report indicated non-detection for petroleum hydrocarbons in nine soil samples collected from the five test pits. 

It is unclear whether a portion or all of the estimated 650 cubic yards of excavated petroleum contaminated soil was used as backfill at the site or removed from the site for disposal.  A “No Further Action” (NFA) determination was issued in October 1990.
